frameworks.name: Three-Option Hate Response Framework
frameworks.definition: A three-level response menu for handling public attacks: (1) Ignore — lowest effort, lets the attacker advertise you for free; (2) Agree — defuse conflict by stepping to the attacker's side; (3) Agree-plus-one — out-insult the attacker by escalating the self-critique beyond what they said.

frameworks.name: Ignore-and-Amplify Strategy
frameworks.definition: When a lie or reputational attack cannot be ignored in silence, combine disciplined non-response with a 10x increase in message volume, drowning the attack via audience share rather than direct rebuttal.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when responding to public attacks or hate, ignoring costs the attacker-defender nothing in time or effort, and that attackers effectively provide free advertising by directing their own audience's attention toward the target — some of whom then become customers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: public-facing creator or business owner with an existing audience
claims.mechanism: The attacker spends their earned attention directing eyeballs at the target; a fraction of those eyeballs convert to customers of the target regardless of intent.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the attack is accompanied by platform deplatforming or legal action that prevents the target from continuing to publish

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that agreeing with an attacker's accusation — even a false or exaggerated one — instantly ends the conflict because conflict requires an equal or opposing force; removing that force leaves the attacker with nothing to push against.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: verbal or social-media attack from an individual or smaller account
claims.mechanism: Conflict is maintained by opposing force; stepping to the attacker's position eliminates the opposition, collapsing the confrontation dynamic.
bounded_by: Less effective when the attack is institutional (legal, regulatory) rather than reputational

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the most powerful response to an attack is to out-insult yourself — escalating the self-critique further than the attacker did — because no one can continue attacking someone who mocks themselves more viciously than the attacker can, and the target appears as the class act while the attacker looks petty.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: attacker is smaller or roughly equal in platform size

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that he has never lost money as a direct result of someone attacking or defaming him online, and that the attack has never reduced his revenue — losses have come only from how people respond to attacks (entering a public conflict that damages them), not from the strength of the attacker.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: attack is from an account or entity smaller in audience reach than the target
bounded_by: Does not cover legal action or regulatory enforcement as a form of attack

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that every moment spent publicly addressing an attacker stops delivering value to one's own audience, and that public figures or businesses are taken down not by the strength of attackers but by how the target responds — because entering a petty conflict with someone below you makes you look bad even when you win.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: attacker is smaller or lower-status than the target
claims.mechanism: A public exchange redistributes audience attention from value content to drama content, lowering perceived status of the larger party and signaling that the attacker can control the target's behavior.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that publicly denying an association — repeatedly stating 'I am not X' — causes audiences to associate the speaker with X over time, because the repetition of the pairing overrides the denial; the more a person defends against a label, the more they reinforce the mental link.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the denial is repeated publicly across multiple posts or statements
claims.mechanism: Brand is built on associations; placing oneself adjacent to any concept — even in denial — conditions the audience to pair the two, regardless of the logical negation.
bounded_by: Does not apply to a single clarifying statement issued once and not repeated

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that hate is a prerequisite for success: the only people who receive no hate are those who are invisible and have taken no position on anything, while anyone who stands for something will attract opposition by necessity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a persistent attacker who receives no response will eventually stop attacking, due to extinction curve dynamics: without reinforcing feedback from the target, the attack behavior is not rewarded and eventually ceases.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the target provides zero response or engagement to the attacker
claims.mechanism: Behavioral extinction: a behavior that produces no reinforcement (feedback, engagement, visible distress) is progressively weakened until it stops. Analogy: yelling at a rock — the rock provides no feedback, so the yelling eventually stops.
bounded_by: Does not apply when a third party (audience or media) reinforces the attacker independently of the target's response

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the only way to combat hate is to drown it out by getting louder with one's own message, not by engaging the attacker directly — because the ratio of positive to negative content consumed by one's audience determines how much the hate registers, and consistent value creation shifts that ratio over time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator or business owner with an active content or communication channel
claims.mechanism: If negative content about a person is 1 day out of 180 days of content, it represents less than 1% of total impressions over that period; the absolute volume of positive content created determines the effective share of mind.

numbers.axis: proportion of negative to total content consumed by audience over time

anchors.region: medium run (6 months of consistent output)
anchors.value: attack is 1-2 days out of 180, i.e. <2% of total impressions

bounded_by: Does not apply if the attacker is a major media institution with orders-of-magnitude more distribution than the target

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that responding to an attacker who is below you in status or audience size signals that the attacker controls your behavior, which displays weakness to your own audience and incentivizes more attacks from others who discover this control mechanism.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the responder has a larger or higher-status audience than the attacker
claims.mechanism: Visible reaction to an attacker communicates that the button works — it reveals a control mechanism that others can exploit. Non-response communicates imperviousness and raises the cost of attacking.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that an individual can only be truly canceled if they either accept being canceled (stop amplifying their message) or are deplatformed from every available channel with no remaining broadcast vehicle; absent those two conditions, continued output eventually outweighs the negative signal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: at least one functional publishing or broadcast channel remains available to the target
bounded_by: Does not hold if the target is simultaneously deplatformed from all channels AND AI content-removal tools suppress third-party coverage

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that hate from others is information about the hater's relative position: hate always originates from below — he reports it has never come from someone more successful or higher-status — and thus receiving hate is a signal that the hater concedes the target's superiority by choosing to follow and react to them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: This is a personal experiential claim, not a population study; counterexamples in competitive markets may exist

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a larger-platform attacker directs their audience at a smaller target, the smaller target benefits by receiving the larger party's audience attention for free — an affiliate-commission-free traffic gift — and the larger party looks petty while the smaller party gains awareness.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the smaller target does not attack back and responds with humor or deflection only
claims.mechanism: The larger party's platform redirects audience attention and awareness to the smaller target; because the smaller target did not pay for this traffic and the larger party funded it, the net effect is an uncompensated audience transfer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that humans are cognitively unequipped to process mass hate at scale because social shame responses evolved for small-group settings; a person receiving 500 hateful comments feels subjectively overwhelmed even though 500 out of 1,000,000 followers represents 0.05% of the audience.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator or public figure with at least tens of thousands of followers
claims.mechanism: Evolutionary social-shame responses calibrated for small-group feedback (village scale) fire at full intensity for each individual hate signal regardless of the signal's proportion to total audience; the denominator is invisible to the emotional system.

numbers.axis: hate signal as percentage of total audience

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that humor is the single most effective counter to hate: a target who makes a joke out of the attack appears fun and high-status, forces the attacker to look petty, and eliminates any remaining attack surface because no one continues attacking someone who laughs at themselves.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the claim of attack is either false or exaggerated enough to be safely mocked
bounded_by: Does not apply to legally serious accusations where flippant humor may be construed as admission or indifference

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that in his personal allocation of response effort, roughly 99% of his attention goes to amplifying his own message and approximately 1% or less goes to any form of direct attack response (agree, agree-plus-one), with ignore being the overwhelmingly dominant strategy.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to Alex Hormozi's personal practice as a content creator and entrepreneur

numbers.axis: share of response effort by response type

examples.text: Alex Hormozi references a scene from the TV show Ted Lasso in which Nate, a former protege, publicly attacks Ted Lasso on live camera, calling him an idiot who doesn't know what he's doing. At the subsequent press conference, Ted responds using the agree-plus-one method: he says Nate could have gone further and mentioned his accent, and then compliments Nate's competitive instincts. The entire press corps laughs. The conflict dissolves because Ted made a joke of the attack and Nate looks vicious for attacking someone with a sense of humor.

Alex Hormozi describes an exchange with a mega-influencer he had followed for years who was being attacked by competitors trying to defame them around a claim central to their brand. The influencer responded with repeated denial posts. Hormozi privately advised: every time you say 'I am not a pink elephant,' people associate you with a pink elephant. He told the influencer the posts were inadvertently amplifying the enemy's message by drawing the influencer's own audience's attention to it. The influencer's following would not stop growing if they simply ignored the attack and kept providing value.

Alex Hormozi describes a major news anchor (top-five outlet) who attacked a content creator in the adult entertainment space by featuring a video of women jumping in a pool and framing it as commentary on the current generation. The creator responded simply: 'You should join us next time.' The anchor looked petty and small; the creator looked fun. The creator reported record sales the following day because the anchor had directed their large platform's attention to the creator for free.

Alex Hormozi describes a female athlete being accused of steroid use. His suggested ideal response: 'Hey guys, you got me. I'm not natural. My boobs are fake. My hair is a darker brown. And my eyelashes — these are fake too. And let me take this makeup remover and smear it off my face — yep, I wear makeup too. So you got me, the rumors are true, I'm not natural, I enhance my appearance.' By out-confessing on adjacent self-enhancement claims the attacker never made, she would have eliminated any remaining attack surface and made the attackers look foolish.

Alex Hormozi shares a story about Layla Hormozi being called a 'skinny bitch' by a man who walked past her. Layla's reaction was to hear it as a compliment — focusing on 'skinny' rather than the insult intent. Hormozi uses this to illustrate that an insult's power over you is determined entirely by how you choose to interpret it, not by the attacker's intent. The same word, received differently, produces a completely different emotional outcome.

practices.text: When attacked publicly, default to ignoring; only escalate to agree or agree-plus-one when the situation specifically benefits from a visible response (e.g., the attack is gaining organic traction that silence would worsen).
Never attack back directly against a hater; use deflection (humor, agreement, self-deprecation) or amplification of your own message rather than direct rebuttal.
When a larger-platform entity attacks you, make a joke out of it and do not return the traffic favor — do not direct your audience toward their platform.

Know your own flaws and embarrassing facts better than any attacker does, so you can out-insult yourself more effectively than they can — keep a mental inventory of self-deprecating material adjacent to likely attack vectors.
Take the anxious energy from being attacked and redirect it into producing more value content — use the emotional activation as fuel for amplification rather than rebuttal.

Focus attention on the 99.9% of the audience who are supportive rather than the 0.1% who are hostile; the supportive majority will organically defend the creator against attackers if given continuous value.
